steps.title: Non-renewable energy resource
steps.body: A resource that will run out one day because it is being used up faster than it can be replaced. Examples: fossil fuels and nuclear fuel.

steps.title: Renewable energy resource
steps.body: A resource that will never run out (or can be replaced within a human lifetime). Examples: solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, biomass, wave.

steps.title: Fossil fuels
steps.body: Coal, oil and natural gas — formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years. They are non-renewable and produce carbon dioxide when burned.

steps.title: Current UK energy mix
steps.body: The UK generates most of its electricity from natural gas, with a growing proportion from renewables (especially wind and solar). Coal use has dropped significantly. Nuclear provides a steady base load.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Worked Example 1 — Evaluating an Energy Source Question: A country is deciding whether to build a new wind farm or a new gas power station. Give two advantages and two disadvantages of each. Solution: Wind farm advantages: No CO₂ emissions, free energy source (wind is free). Disadvantages: Unreliable (needs wind), visual and noise pollution. Gas power station advantages: Reliable (can produce electricity on demand), can respond quickly to changes in demand. Disadvantages: Releases CO₂ (contributes to climate change), fuel must be purchased (running costs). steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When comparing energy sources, always give both advantages AND disadvantages — exam questions often ask you to evaluate or discuss. Use the correct terms: reliable means it can provide energy on demand; renewable means it will not run out. If asked "why do we still use fossil fuels?", the key points are: reliability, existing infrastructure, cost . If asked "why switch to renewables?", the key points are: finite resources, climate change, pollution . Biomass is carbon neutral — be prepared to explain this using photosynthesis and the carbon cycle. Always consider the full picture — not just whether a source is renewable, but also reliability, cost, and environmental impact.
